newsitem.title: UK: Stg Eurobond market set to improve after election.
newsitem.headline: Stg Eurobond market set to improve after election.

text.p: Demand for sterling Eurobonds looks set to improve after the British election on Thursday, but bankers said activity was unlikely to return to the heady pace seen in January.

"The election has created an element of uncertainty that has tended to inhibit business, and that has led to some pent-up demand from issuers to issue and investors to invest," said one syndicate manager.
"Sentiment is still good, though off its peaks. But the market could get an injection of confidence once this election is out of the way," another added.
Financial markets have already factored in a victory by the Labour Party, well ahead in opinion polls, and an interest rate hike of either 25 or 50 basis points, they said.

Spreads on both the long and short end are holding steady, but they said, there appears to be more scope for spreads to tighten on the short end because of sterling, which is holding near four-year highs against the mark.
The currency generally is expected to maintain its strength, largely because it is the one most likely to opt out of the European currency union in the first wave in 1999.
"Sterling is likely to remain outside of the tensions that other currencies will experience over the next two years," said a syndicate manager with another major brokerage.
That, combined with expectations for higher British interest rates, means the British currency will probably remain buoyant over the near-term, they said.

"It's a stand-off between buying expensive sterling and benefiting from historically high UK rates (versus Europe) and it's not an easy judgement to make," he added. "But I think contentintal European investors will come back into the market and buy after the election."

Issuance volumes of sterling Eurobonds surged in the first quarter of 1997, with European retail investors attracted by the yield pick-up over other European currencies and the strength of the currency.
More than $26 billion equivalent of new bonds were launched, compared with $14 billion in the first quarter of 1996, Capital DATA Bondware figures showed.

Both investors and borrowers have moved to the sidelines in the weeks leading up to the election, and while activity is likely to pick up after the election, no one was forecasting a rush of new issues either.
"There's won't be a flood, but broadly speaking, rates are still attractive for issuers," said another.
Most new issues were expected on the short end.

They said new issues could emerge from the British utility sector later this year if the Labour Party wins the election and levies a larger-than-expected windfall tax. They said some may fund the windfall tax through new issues, which typically are dated 10 years or longer.
The market, they added, could easily absorb such deals.
